echoes.note: Daniel alone perceives the vision while the men with him do not see it but flee in terror; he then falls to the ground. Acts 9:7's companions 'stood speechless, hearing the sound but seeing no one' is the same selective-perception convention attached to an overwhelming theophany, with the seer prostrate. Volume and thematic coherence are strong; the divergence (companions hear vs. do not see) is exactly the kind of variation Luke replays in his retellings (cf. ch. 22, 26).

The appearance of the glory of the LORD as radiant brightness causes Ezekiel to fall on his face and hear a voice speaking. Saul's 'light from the sky,' falling to the earth, and a speaking voice replays the Kavod-theophany sequence. High thematic coherence with the prophetic call pattern; verbal volume is moderate (light/glory, fell, voice).

After Ezekiel falls, the voice commands 'Son of man, stand on your feet... I send you to the people.' Saul is told to 'rise up, and enter into the city,' the same fall-then-rise-and-go commissioning rhythm. Coherence with the immediately following sending to the nations is strong; verbal borrowing modest.

'Moses, Moses' — the doubled-vocative call from a blazing divine manifestation, answered before commission. 'Saul, Saul' matches the convention. Recurrence is strong across the OT call type-scenes (Gen 22:11; 46:2; 1 Sam 3:10), which strengthens rather than dilutes the echo.

The throne-vision call of Isaiah — overwhelmed prophet confronted by divine glory, then sent — is the archetype Luke draws Saul's commissioning into. Little verbal overlap, but the type-scene logic (theophany → unworthiness → sending) is the figural frame; coherence high, volume low.

Jeremiah is appointed 'a prophet to the nations' before birth; the Damascus call culminates (v.15) in Saul as the chosen vessel 'before the nations.' The conversion proper carries this only faintly; the nations-prophet resonance lands more in vv.10-19. Low volume here.

A dread/darkness falls upon Abram at a covenant theophany; Saul is plunged into three days of darkness. Faint, contested — the motif of incapacitating darkness accompanying divine encounter, but no verbal contact.

The LORD calls 'Ananias!' in a vision and he answers 'Behold, it's me, Lord' — the Samuel night-call type-scene, where the named summons is met with hinneni ('Here I am'). High coherence with the prophetic-vision call form; the responsive formula is the load-bearing parallel.

The Servant is named from the womb to be 'a light to the nations,' and kings shall see (49:7). The Lord's word that Saul is 'my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel' fuses the Servant's mission to nations + kings + Israel. Strong thematic coherence; Luke is casting Saul in the Isaianic Servant role.

Tobit's blindness is healed when the white films/scales peel from the corners of his eyes and he recovers his sight. 'Something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight' is strikingly close in image and vocabulary (the scaling-off of a film). Deuterocanonical; high volume on the distinctive scales-from-eyes motif.

Elisha prays and the LORD strikes the Aramean army with blindness, leads them into Damascus, then prays again that their eyes be opened and they see. Saul is struck blind, led by the hand into Damascus, and his eyes opened there. The Damascus setting plus blinding/opening-of-eyes makes this more than coincidental; medium for moderate verbal contact.

Ananias's hesitant objection ('Lord, I have heard... how much evil he did') and the Lord's overriding 'Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel' replays the prophetic objection-and-reassurance pattern (Jer 1:6 'Ah, Lord'; cf. Exod 3:11; 4:1). Coherence high with the call form; verbal volume modest.

The 'chosen vessel' image may draw on the potter-and-clay vessel that God refashions to his purpose. Faint and contested — Luke's skeuos eklogēs evokes the vessel-of-election idea but without verbal anchoring to the potter oracle specifically.

Those plotting to kill watch the gates day and night, but Saul's disciples 'let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket' by night — exactly as Michal lets David down through a window so he can escape the men watching the house to kill him. The conjunction of murderous watch + nocturnal lowering-down escape is the strongest single parallel.

Rahab lets the spies down by a rope through her window because her house was built into the city wall. 'Let him down through the wall' matches the lowering-through-the-wall escape motif precisely; high volume on the wall + lowering imagery.

The psalm (titled to David's escape while enemies 'watched the house to kill him') pleads for deliverance from those who lie in wait. The 'watched the gates day and night to kill him' language resonates with the persecuted-righteous-one motif. Low volume, contested.

The summary that the churches were 'walking in the fear of the Lord' and were built up draws on the wisdom idiom of life ordered by the fear of the LORD. Diffuse stock biblical phrase; low volume, no single source.

Peter's command to the bedridden Aeneas, 'Get up and make your bed,' reverses the prophetic word that one will not 'come down from the bed' to which he has gone up. Faint thematic inversion of the bed-of-affliction motif from the Elijah cycle; low and contested.

The healing of the paralytic so that he immediately rises belongs to the prophetic vision of the lame leaping when God restores his people; 'all who lived at Lydda... turned to the Lord' fits the restoration-and-return frame. Low volume, no verbal borrowing.

Elisha enters the room where the dead child lies, puts everyone out, prays, and the child opens her/his eyes. 'Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed... he said, Tabitha, get up! She opened her eyes' matches the sequence point-for-point: privacy, prayer, command, the opening of the eyes. Highest-volume parallel in the pericope.

Elijah raises the widow's son, who is laid in the upper room (loft) where the prophet prays; the result is faith ('now I know'). Tabitha is laid in an upper room, surrounded by widows, raised through Peter's prayer, and 'many believed.' Strong coherence: upper room + widow context + prayer + resurrection + resulting belief.

Beyond the resuscitation itself, the Shunammite cycle frames the dead one laid in a prepared upper chamber and messengers sent urgently to fetch the man of God ('do not slacken your riding'); Joppa's disciples 'sent two men... imploring him not to delay.' The send-for-the-prophet-without-delay motif reinforces the Elisha typology.
